slides.headline: This shrimp punches like a bullet.
slides.sub: 5 facts about the peacock mantis shrimp that sound made up

slides.headline: Its club accelerates faster than a .22 bullet
slides.body: The strike reaches ~23 m/s with acceleration over 10,000 g, the fastest recorded limb movement of any animal.

slides.label: peak force in a single strike
slides.body: That's thousands of times its own body weight. Aquarium keepers have lost glass tanks to them.

slides.headline: The punch is so fast it boils water
slides.body: The club moves fast enough to create cavitation bubbles. When they collapse, they release heat, light and a second shockwave, so prey gets hit twice.

slides.headline: 12 colour receptors. We have 3.
slides.body: Yet they are worse at telling colours apart than we are. They likely use a fast 'colour lookup' instead of comparing signals like our brains do.

slides.headline: They can see circularly polarised light
slides.body: One of the only animals known to do so. They appear to use it for private signalling that predators can't read.

slides.headline: Save this for later.
slides.body: A new species, properly sourced, every week. Follow @earthspirit_nature.

caption:
The peacock mantis shrimp (Odontodactylus scyllarus) is 10–18 cm long and can crack a crab shell (or an aquarium wall) with a strike that accelerates faster than a bullet.

Swipe for 4 facts that sound invented but come straight from peer-reviewed research (sources on the last slide).

Photos: Diego Delso, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (links on last slide).
